title: A three-planet model fits 2019-2026 TOI-682 timings with planet c near 16.134 days under fixed RV inputs
abstract: We test whether a third planet can explain TOI-682 b transit timing variations while the reported RV planet c stays near 16.134 days. We use 23 published times from 2019 to 2026 and one transit-shape constraint. We first resolve a prior six-minute difference between TTVFast and REBOUND: their default Jacobi element inputs use different mass conventions. The same Cartesian initial state gives agreement below 0.0064 seconds for all 22 published two-planet examples. We then run 24 local three-planet searches, refinements, and two added tests. One model has chi-square 16.935 for 13 nominal degrees of freedom. Its c has a fixed initial period of 16.134 days and a mean conjunction period of 16.13205 days. Its third planet d has a mean period of 27.12937 days, mass 28.43 Earth masses, eccentricity 0.0447, and predicted RV semi-amplitude 6.18 m/s. Both c and d miss the star in the tested geometry. The model remains bound for 18,724 years in two Newtonian integrations with different time steps; the finer run has sampled fractional energy error below 2.1e-8. Other good timing examples trigger a numerical close-distance screen. Thus a concrete third-planet model can retain the RV period near its reported value. This is not a detection or a fit to individual RVs. Limits include fixed poster inputs without errors, inherited timing and shape results, incomplete local searches, no full light-curve or RV likelihood, and finite Newtonian survival tests. We preserve the Cartesian states, forecasts, failed fits, source hashes and reproduction code.

display.caption: One conditional three-planet timing fit, selected transit forecasts, and the full predicted stellar velocity. The model predicts an extra RV signal near 27.13 days. These are point examples, not posterior intervals or a planet detection.
The two dynamics codes use different mass conventions for their default Jacobi element input. A Cartesian transfer gives agreement within milliseconds for 22 published point solutions.
